title: Refactoring Code Smells to Patterns: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on spotting the classic code smells (long method, large class, switch statements, shotgun surgery, feature envy, primitive obsession) and removing them with Strategy, State, Factory and Template Method refactorings in small, safe, test-backed steps.

chapters.title: Code Smells: The Mental Model
points: A code smell is a surface symptom that hints at a deeper design problem; the code works, but it is costly to change. A smell is a prompt to investigate, not a bug
Refactoring = changing internal structure without changing observable behavior; it is always done with passing tests as the safety net
Smells group by cost: bloaters (long method, large class, primitive obsession), change preventers (shotgun surgery, divergent change), couplers (feature envy)
Smell vs bug: a bug breaks behavior now; a smell makes the next change risky, slow or expensive
Mistake: refactoring and adding a feature in the same commit, so a failing test cannot be traced to one cause

chapters.title: Bloaters and Couplers: Spotting the Six Smells
points: Long Method: does several things at different abstraction levels; signs are comments marking sections and 20+ lines; fix with Extract Method
Large Class: too many fields and responsibilities, so it changes for many unrelated reasons (violates SRP); fix with Extract Class
Switch Statements: the same type-code switch or if/else chain repeated in many places; adding a new type means editing every copy (violates Open/Closed)

Shotgun Surgery: one logical change forces small edits across many classes; opposite of Large Class (Divergent Change is one class edited for many reasons); fix with Move Method and Inline Class to gather the logic
Feature Envy: a method uses another object's data more than its own (a.getB().getC().getX() chains); fix with Move Method to the class that owns the data

chapters.title: Primitive Obsession and Cohesion
points: Primitive Obsession: using String, int or double for domain ideas (money, email, phone, status code) so validation and behavior scatter across callers
Fix with Replace Primitive with Value Object: e.g. Money(amount, currency) is immutable, validates in its constructor and owns add() and format()
Replace type-code ints and strings with an enum or class so illegal values cannot compile; a type code that drives behavior needs polymorphism (State or Strategy) instead
Data Clumps (the same 3 params travel together, like start, end, timezone) become one parameter object, which also shortens long parameter lists
Mistake: wrapping every primitive in a class; wrap only values with rules, invariants or behavior

chapters.title: Refactoring to Strategy, State and Template Method
points: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism: each switch branch becomes a subclass or implementation of a common interface; the switch disappears from the callers

Strategy: the client picks an interchangeable algorithm (e.g. ShippingCost: Standard, Express); the context holds a Strategy reference and delegates; the algorithm does not change during the object's life

State: the object itself changes behavior as its internal state changes (Order: Pending, Paid, Shipped); each State class handles transitions and returns the next state; replaces boolean flags and status switches
Strategy vs State: identical class shape; Strategy is chosen from outside and states do not know each other, State is switched from inside and states know their successors

Template Method: a base class fixes the algorithm skeleton as a final method calling abstract steps (parse, validate, save); subclasses fill in the steps; use it when duplicated flows differ only in a few steps, and prefer Strategy when you need runtime swapping or composition over inheritance

chapters.title: Factory and Small Safe Refactoring Steps
points: Factory (Replace Constructor with Factory Method): one place holds the single remaining switch that maps a type code to a Strategy or State object, so callers never use new on concrete classes
Safe step loop: run tests green, make ONE small mechanical change, run tests again, commit; if red, revert instead of debugging a big change
Characterization tests: before refactoring untested code, write tests that pin down current behavior, even odd behavior, so you can detect accidental changes

Safe order for a switch smell: Extract Method for each branch, Move Method into a class, introduce the interface, one branch at a time; the old switch and the new classes coexist until the last branch moves (Branch by Abstraction)

Mistakes: big-bang rewrite, changing behavior and structure together, skipping tests, abstracting after one case (wait for the 2nd or 3rd duplicate, the Rule of Three), and a Factory that still has a switch in many places

chapters.title: Refactoring Cheat Sheet
points: Smell to fix: Long Method → Extract Method; Large Class → Extract Class; Switch → Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
Smell to fix: Shotgun Surgery → Move Method / Inline Class; Feature Envy → Move Method; Primitive Obsession → Value Object / enum
Pattern pick: algorithm chosen by client → Strategy; behavior driven by object's own lifecycle → State; fixed skeleton with varying steps → Template Method; creation by type code → Factory
Loop: green tests → one small step → green tests → commit; red means revert; no feature work in a refactor commit
Interview Point: Strategy vs State? Shotgun Surgery vs Divergent Change? Why characterization tests before refactoring? When is a Factory switch acceptable? Template Method vs Strategy trade-off?
